steps.summary: Classical Ionic columns with fluted shafts supporting the entablature
Letters spelling 'KENT' on the entablature
Partially visible text that appears to read 'IUS EST ARS' or similar in Latin on the stone band between the entablature and the windows
Red brick facade with light-colored stone trim and architectural details
Arched black doorway with transom window and fanlight above
Three rectangular windows with light-colored frames and blue shades/reflections
Decorative dentil molding and repeating pattern in the entablature above 'KENT'
Rectangular recessed panels on either side of the doorway below the windows
Two classical Ionic columns with white marble or stone appearance
Red brick or paved ground level at the base of the facade
Patterned red and white brick or stone stripe pattern visible at the very top of the image above the entablature

The building bears the word 'KENT' prominently on its entablature (e2), and the Latin phrase 'Ius est ars boni et aequi' (law is the art of goodness and fairness) is a classic legal motto often found on courthouses (e3). This strongly suggests a courthouse for a place named 'Kent' - likely Kent County. There are several Kent Counties (Delaware, Michigan, Rhode Island, England). Given the classical American courthouse architecture with red brick and Ionic columns, and a 'book return' box visible at bottom left suggesting this may actually be a library rather than courthouse - possibly Kent State University or a Kent County building. The style is consistent with early 20th century Beaux-Arts civic architecture common in the northeastern US. Kent County, Delaware's courthouse in Dover is a strong candidate given similar architecture.
